title: Mechanisms of emergence from general anesthesia
text:
Millions of people experience general anesthesia each year in the United States, yet the mechanisms governing
anesthetic actions are unclear. The period of arousal from anesthesia, termed emergence, is a particularly
sensitive and dangerous time in clinical anesthesia care, and no therapeutic strategy currently exists for
modifying emergence. This proposal aims to elucidate inhibitory cellular, circuit, and behavioral mechanisms of
emergence from general anesthesia in order to inform the development of mechanistically targeted interventions.

title: Understanding the Roles of Synovitis, Knee-Adjacent Obesity and Sarcopenia in Pain Phenotypes and Structural Progression of Knee Osteoarthritis - An Analysis of the Entire Osteoarthritis Initiative
text:
(Public Health Relevance)
Obesity, muscle mass, and joint inflammation are modifiable risk factors for osteoarthritis (OA); however, there
is a knowledge gap on how these risk factors impact pain and structural outcomes, which is crucial for managing
OA and influencing quality of life and mobility. Moreover, it is not well known how related weight change, co-
morbidities, lifestyle factors (such as diet), and physical activity mediate the progression of OA. The overall goal
of this proposal is, therefore, to elucidate the mechanisms responsible for pain and structural progression of OA
focusing on modifiable risk factors such as inflammation, local body composition, and sarcopenia and to develop
a clinically applicable prediction model for pain and structural outcomes, thus building a foundation for targeted
and individualized treatment plans.

title: Defining the mechanistic basis of the airway metaplastic response: the roles of stem cell heterogeneity, Yap, and EGFR signaling
text:
Although squamous and mucous metaplasia are the two main forms of pathologic epithelial injury response
in airway disease, the cellular source and molecular mechanisms governing their formation have not been
clearly defined. Understanding how recently discovered heterogenous stem cell populations in distinct
anatomic regions of the airway contribute to squamous and mucous metaplasia, and further establishing
how these stem cells interact with disease-associated signaling pathways will inform strategies to mitigate
pathologic metaplasia.

title: CTSA RC2 Program at University of Utah: A Translational Platform for Rapid Genomic Medicine
text:
The goal of this Specialized Innovation Program is to identify and overcome barriers that impede the
translational science of rapid genomic medicine discoveries at the point of care by assembling the
infrastructure, technology, and strategies to design and develop a rapid genomic diagnostic platform, using the
newborn intensive care unit as our laboratory. We will design and develop an innovative, collaborative, patient-
focused, and electronic health record-interfaced translational platform that efficiently integrates rapid genomic
medicine at the point of care.

title: Photoreceptor cell death and survival in retinal degeneration
text: This research aims to understand programmed cell death/survival in mouse models of retinal degeneration and to identify cellular pathways that promote cell survival. Living-color reporters named CaspBiosensors will be used to identify cells that will eventually die (susceptible) and other cells that are reverse their death signal (well-surviving). The cellular and molecular features of these susceptible/well-surviving cells will be investigated to inform the development of neuroprotection therapies.

title: Developing a Cancer Galaxy Computational Workbench to Meet Emerging Cancer Data Analysis Needs
text:
Computational data analyses have become essential in cancer research, but technical challenges make these
data analyses difficult for many cancer researchers. We will develop the Galaxy-C software platform to make it
easier for all cancer researchers—especially those with limited informatics expertise—to perform
computational data analyses. The Galaxy-C software platform will help cancer researchers perform accurate,
robust, and efficient computational data analyses.

title: Genetics Predoctoral Training Program
text: The Genetics Predoctoral Training Program (GPTP) at Emory University trains students in genetics, genomics and molecular biology. Through a rigorous yet flexible curriculum, dissertation research and customized career development training plans aligned to individual student competency-based assessments, students are prepared to obtain and succeed in the career of their choice within the biomedical workforce.

title: Antagonism and neurocomputational mechanisms of cooperation
text:
This study aims to better understand the "dark" side of human personality, including antisociality and
narcissism, by exploring how the brain learns from our interactions with others. By examining brain
mechanisms involved in social learning and cooperation, we hope to gain new insights into conditions such as
conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, substance use disorders, and antisocial, narcissistic,
borderline, and histrionic personality disorders. The findings could lead to more personalized treatments based
on an individual’s interpersonal patterns, identified through questionnaires, interviews, and brain activity.

title: High Dimensional Data Analysis Core
text: CORE C - ABSTRACT – High Dimensional Data Analysis Core The purpose of this core is to manage and support the resources to address fundamental questions about the development of the airway epithelium and the role that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) plays in childhood respiratory morbidity and asthma. This data management and analysis core will serve to manage the data from the unique longitudinal human study population, Childhood Asthma and the Neonatal Epithelium – Vanderbilt University (CANOE-VU), and will provide bioinformatic and biostatistical support for the analysis of longitudinal multi-modal omics data in Project 1, and the proposed mechanistic studies in Project 2. The combination of data management and analysis centered within one core allows for the oversight of the complex human, biosample and experimental data to be used in this proposal, and the integrated collaboration of the biostatistical and bioinformatics teams in the proposed analyses and thus builds synergy for the Projects 1 and 2 that this core serves. This core assembles a highly collaborative research team of biostatisticians, geneticists, systems biologists, bioinformaticians and database management specialists with complementary expertise in working with complex multi-dimensional data along with the specific data management and state- of-the-art analytical skills necessary to successfully conduct the proposed studies. The major functions of the core, data management and data analysis, are outlined in three separate aims or functions of this core: (1) Management and curation of clinical, physiological and airway epithelium multi-omic data across collaborating sites with a central infrastructure to facilitate the proposed research. This includes ensuring subject-level data quality control of primary clinical data collection, the pre-analytical variables and biospecimen processing and performance of assays with validated standard protocols that minimize errors in reproducibility, and efficient organization of samples and data among all research centers; (2) Coordination of bioinformatics analysis, integration and validation of multi-omics data across projects. This aim specifically exists to address unique challenges posed by analysis of longitudinal data in multi-dimensional space, for which there is little precedent in the field. A robust integrated approach to longitudinal analysis of multi-omic data has been developed and will be implemented across sites as described in this core’s strategy; (3) Provide analytic support for the conduct of rigorous biostatistical analyses to address research questions across Projects 1 and 2. This aim will provide centralized biostatistical analysis support and will address statistical challenges and solutions common to statistical analysis components of both projects. This is a natural extension of the work of our experienced data science team who have been integrated into each of the projects, and who will oversee the proposed analyses, assuring rigor and reproducibility.

title: Establishing the impact of disease-associated KCNH1 mutations on neuronal physiology
text:
Mutations in the KCNH1 gene have been associated with Temple‐Baraitser and Zimmermann‐Laband, two
overlapping syndromes characterized by impaired neurodevelopment and frequent epileptic seizures. However,
the impact of the mutant KCNH1 on human neuronal physiology remains unexplored. Here, we will use iPSC-
based technologies and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to establish human models of these diseases, determine
the mechanisms of neuronal dysfunction and develop antisense oligonucleotide-based therapeutics.

title: Stromal Effects in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
text:
Project Narrative/Public Health Relevance Statement
The heterogeneity of tumor microenvironment provides a unique physiological milieu for tumor progression and
metastasis. The findings of this proposal will reveal a stromal progenitor cell hierarchy in squamous cell
carcinoma to provide a foundation for cancer organoid culture, high-throughput screening, personalized
medicine, and biomarker identification in head and neck cancer. The long-term goal of this proposal is to
develop an applicable model to achieve the cure of cancer.

title: Core C: Atherosclerosis and bioinformatics core
text: Abstract The Atherosclerosis and Bioinformatics Core (Core C) within the Program Project grant “Triglycerides, Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease” will provide all three individual Projects with expertise in pathology- based analytical techniques to evaluate atherosclerotic lesions. Techniques include histological staining and immunohistochemistry. The Core will also provide expertise in RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, and CITE-seq bioinformatics analyses as a complement to the Program Project investigators’ projects. This Core’s repertoire of high-quality analyses of atherosclerosis will substantially enhance the scientific progress of the three individual projects.

title: Targeting melanoma promoting RNA modification pathway for melanoma therapy.
text:
PUBLIC HEALTH SIGNIFICANCE
Metastatic melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer that accounts for 8,000 deaths annually in the United
States alone and currently approved therapies including BRAF/MEK targeted therapies and immune
checkpoint blockade therapies benefit only a subset of metastatic melanoma patients. We have discovered
that YTHDF1, a reader of m6A-modified mRNA, as a driver of melanoma metastasis and demonstrated that
two downstream mediators of YTHDF1 function, the TrkB/BDNF and the metabolic enzyme IMPDH1, can be
pharmacologically inhibited for metastatic melanoma therapy. Our proposed studies will establish YTHDF1 as
a novel driver of melanoma metastasis, identify new mechanisms by which it facilitates melanoma metastasis,
and ascertain the efficacy of small-molecule inhibitors of TrkB/BDNF and IMPDH1 for treating both naïve and
drug resistant metastatic melanoma.

title: UT Southwestern Medical Center Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center
text:
OVERALL
PROJECT NARRATIVE
The mission of the Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center (SCCC) is to reduce the burden of cancer through
transformational science and innovative therapies, an emphasis on prevention, patient-centered care, and
cancer health disparities, and a culture of community engagement, all aiming to impact public health. Goals of
our 2025 – 2030 Strategic Plan “Translational Cancer Research for Community Benefit” are to enable
bidirectional translational cancer science weaving the domains of the laboratory, the clinic, and the community;
transdisciplinary research programs; and, through improvements in public health, transformation of the cancer
burden in the SCCC catchment area and beyond.

title: Project 1: Combine Viro-Immunotherapy and Natural Killer Cells for the Treatment of Gliomas
text:
PROJECT 1
In a recent paradigm shift, oncolytic adenoviruses are recognized as new type of cancer immunotherapy,
suggesting that oncolytic viruses may have powerful synergistic effects when combined with other
immunotherapeutic strategies. In this project, we explore in pre-clinical models the biological effects of combining
our novel oncolytic adenovirus, Delta-24-RGD, with home-grown genetically engineered, immunosuppression-
resistant natural killer cells (called eCB-NK-TR-/GC- cells). We test in two sequential Phase 1 window-of-
opportunity clinical trials the safety, efficacy and biological effects of eCB-NK-TR-/GC- cells alone and in
combination with Delta-24-RGD in patients with recurrent glioblastoma.

title: Research Program: Genome Regulation and Cell Signaling
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – GENOME REGULATION AND CELL SIGNALING PROGRAM The Genome Regulation and Cell Signaling (GRCS) Program at the Wistar Cancer Center elucidates basic mechanisms of cancer gene expression, signaling, and immune reprogramming. GRCS was launched in 2024 as part of a strategic realignment of Cancer Center Programs to enhance transdisciplinary collaboration and basic-to-clinical translation of cancer research. Building on the full, collaborative alignment between Wistar's Vaccine and Immunotherapy Center (VIC) and the Cancer Center, the former Immunology, Microenvironment and Metastasis (IMM) Program was terminated, new interdisciplinary research themes of cancer signaling, immunotherapy, and drug discovery were included in the former Gene Expression and Regulation (GER) Program and a new GRCS Program was created. Compared to the GER Program, which was rated Outstanding to Exceptional at the 2018 Cancer Center Support Grant (CCSG) renewal, GRCS is more scientifically impactful with increased membership (17 vs. 8 members), larger funding base ($6.4 million vs. $4.9 million) and greater peer-reviewed cancer-related funding ($5.3 million vs. $3.4 million). NCI funding currently stands at $2.1 million, translating into a strong cancer focus of 40%. The Program is highly collaborative, with one Specialized Program of Research Excellence (SPORE) in ovarian cancer (P50 CA228991), two program project grants on Epstein- Barr Virus (EBV)-induced lymphoma (P01 CA281867) and epithelial malignancies (P01 CA269043), one consortium grant on the EBV methylome (U01 CA284811), and eight multi-investigator R01 awards. As a result, 63% of peer-reviewed cancer-related funding and 49% of discovery publications (excluding reviews, commentaries and method papers) are the product of collaboration. Fulfilling its foundational goal of basic-to- clinical translational cancer research, GRCS discoveries in EBV-directed oncogenesis (Lieberman), mitochondria-induced tumor plasticity (Altieri), cancer-associated neoepitopes (Weiner) and HPV vaccination (Weiner) have advanced to collaborative, first-in-human oncology clinical trials. Currently, the Program is co-led by internationally renowned research leaders in oncogenic viruses and drug discovery (Lieberman, Leader) and RNA biology (Tian, co-Leader), coalescing its members around three flagship research themes: (i) chromatin biology and RNA metabolism; (ii) cancer and immune cell signaling; and (iii) tumor virology and immunology. Reflecting multidisciplinary approaches in basic and translational cancer research, GRCS Program members utilize a broad array of state-of-the-art technologies in molecular, cellular and chemical biology, immunology, and computational and systems biology, are heavy users of all eight CCSG-supported Shared Resources and are leaders in the education, training and mentoring of junior investigators. Building on these transformative achievements, the GRCS Program is now ideally poised to enable the historic expansion of the Cancer Center in the next five years, as a catalyst of transdisciplinary collaboration with the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis (MCO) Program and the new, cancer-focused Center for Advanced Therapeutics.

title: Mechanism and Countermeasure of Fentanyl-Induced Sudden Death
text: Overdose fentanyl via rapid intravenous injection causes sudden death, which is the deadliest in opioid overdose deaths, but the relevant pathophysiological mechanisms and effective countermeasures are still unknown. The proposed study will establish the first animal model of fentanyl-induced sudden death and thereby further determine the pathogenesis of the sudden death and a corresponding countermeasure.

title: Biophysical Imaging
text: The principal objective of the Biophysical Imaging Core is to provide PPG investigators with a complete range of expertise, training, equipment, and data analysis tools to obtain nano-to-micro scale biophysical information pertaining to the cellular and molecular basis of endothelial cell (EC) cytoskeletal rearrangements and barrier regulation. Core D personnel and equipment will allow PPG scientists to image 3D structures, evaluate physi- cal and chemical properties and define perturbant-induced real-time changes in the structures and activity of cells and subcellular constituents, including membranes, cytoskeletal networks, cell-matrix and cell-cell junc- tions. This Biophysical Imaging Core supports the PPG's four research projects with quantitative microscopy related to atomic force microscopy (AFM), confocal and deconvolution fluorescence microscopy, total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, dynamic (live) fluorescence imaging, mechanical measurements of cells (traction force microscopy), super-resolution microscopy and automated high-throughput quantitative mi- croscopy to allow observation of cellular organelles (e.g., cortical cytoskeleton, junctional complexes, focal ad- hesions and lamellipodia) in great detail (3D). Core D will also interact with each Project and with Core B (Ge- nomic/Genetic and Proteome Core) to culture endothelial cells engineered to express different nmMLCK1/2, cortactin, NAMPT, TLR4, DOCK1, lamellipodin, integrin β4, kindlin-2, PSGL1, P-Selectin and S1PR1/3 recep- tors transgenes with specific SNP or post-translational modification mutations and measure various biophysical forces (TFM and AFM). The Core also offers access to experienced use of the complete resources of the Uni- versity of Arizona Imaging Core Facilities that includes state-of-the-art high-resolution fluorescence microscopy systems. This Core will also make use of the common resources available at Arizona Research Laboratories. The Biophysical Imaging Core, led by Carol C. Gregorio, PhD, includes personnel and laboratory facilities for a wide range dynamic fluorescence imaging, fabrication, and mechanobiophysics. Core D personnel have pro- fessional experience spanning the fields of high-resolution imaging and examining physical and chemical properties, including mechanobiophysics, and various scanning probe microscopies. All Core D experiments will be conducted at the University of Arizona in Tucson.

title: Research Specialist Support- Establishing and Interpreting Abnormal DNA Methylation in Cancer
text:
This renewal proposal aims to support Dr. Minmin Liu as a Research Specialist, enabling her to cultivate a stable
and thriving career critical to Dr. Peter A. Jones's research program in the field of cancer epigenetics. Dr. Liu is
uniquely qualified due to her strong research background, expertise in next-generation sequencing techniques,
and computational data analysis for epigenetic/epigenomic studies, as well as her track record of making
significant scientific contributions. Dr. Liu's proficiency will integrate cellular, biochemical, structural, and animal
studies to elucidate how abnormal DNA methylation is established and interpreted in cancer cells.

title: Neural mechanisms of memory consolidation in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex
text:
Memory is an essential cognitive function, but little is known about how the brain stores long-term memories and
extracts knowledge from past experience. An understanding of these neural processes, called memory
consolidation, would provide important foundational knowledge for understanding how consolidation may be
altered in disease. This study investigates neural substrates of memory consolidation with a focus on the
hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex, two brain regions important for memory and implicated in a range of
neuropsychiatric conditions.
